item.text: I’ve got enough: the strongest positives are institutional reform, rule-based budgeting, and universal child-policy design; the main negatives are incomplete rights institutions and persistent equality/justice gaps.

**6B.9 Research Note**

Overall: **moderately yes, but incomplete**. Kishida’s 2024 strongest institution-building was process-heavy and likely to outlast him: political-funds oversight, external audits, EBPM/medium-term budget rules, universal child support, and local-service grants. The main gap is that Japan still lacked stronger independent rights institutions, and some equality deficits remained structural rather than solved.

**Positive**
- **Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | June 21, 2024 | https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202406/21kaiken.html | Kishida said his reform headquarters had already pushed core measures, the Political Funds Control Act was amended, and the next step was a third-party body for inspections and audits. That is durable institutional design beyond a one-off political fix. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.7`, `6B.5`
- **Policy Speech by Prime Minister Kishida to the 213th Session of the Diet** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | January 30, 2024 | https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202401/30shiseihoshin.html | Kishida tied child policy, fiscal policy, and political reform to transparency, compliance, and legal change, indicating an effort to lock reforms into formal rules rather than personal discretion. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.7`, `6B.4`, `6B.5`
- **Meeting of the Council on Economic and Fiscal Policy** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | July 29, 2024 | https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/actions/202407/29keizai.html | Kishida explicitly endorsed medium- to long-term projections, continuing spending reform, and strengthening EBPM and “wise spending,” which is the clearest evidence of durable rule-based policy machinery. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.5`, `5B.10`
- **Policies supporting children and child-rearing** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | 2024 page content | https://japan.kantei.go.jp/ongoingtopics/policies_kishida/childsupport.html | The child-support package is laid out as universal and income-independent, with fixed benefits and administrative entitlements rather than ad hoc favors, making it a durable social institution if maintained. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.8`, `6B.7`, `6B.4`
- **Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida on the Noto response** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | July 1, 2024 | https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202407/01kaiken.html | Kishida described repeated reserve-fund tranches restoring infrastructure, lifelines, housing, and livelihoods, which suggests a routinized state recovery capacity rather than personal charity. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.6`, `6B.4`, `6B.5`
- **Video Message by Prime Minister Kishida at the Symposium on Inclusive Society and Human Rights** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | February 5, 2024 | https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202402/05_message.html | He anchored policy in human dignity, rule of law, and anti-discrimination norms, which supports the existence of a rights-bearing institutional order rather than a leader-centered patronage system. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.8`, `6B.3`

**Mixed / Negative**
- **World Report 2024: Japan** | Human Rights Watch | 2024 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/japan | HRW said Japan still lacked a national human rights institution and that criminal justice remained abusive, showing Kishida had not yet built durable rights-protecting institutions robust enough to survive him unchanged. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.8`, `6B.5`, `6B.7`
- **Japan: Freedom in the World 2024 Country Report** | Freedom House | 2024 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/japan/freedom-world/2024 | Freedom House notes continuing underrepresentation of women, exclusion of some ethnic Koreans from elections because of citizenship rules, and persistent equality gaps for LGBT people and asylum seekers, so the institutional settlement remained incomplete. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.8`, `6B.2`, `6B.3`
- **Japan: Freedom on the Net 2024 Country Report** | Freedom House | 2024 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/japan/freedom-net/2024 | Freedom House says government pressure and the kisha kurabu system contribute to self-censorship and restricted access, which weakens the case that Kishida left behind fully durable, self-correcting public institutions. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.8`, `6B.5`
- **Japan PM Kishida won’t run for reelection at LDP race, Kyodo reports** | Reuters | August 14, 2024 | https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/japan-pm-kishida-wont-run-for-reelection-at-ldp-race-kyodo-reports-3570455 | Reuters framed Kishida’s exit as driven by scandal and living-cost anger, which suggests his reform program was still politically fragile and not yet fully institutionalized beyond his own tenure. | QIDs: `6B.9`, `6B.7`, `5B.5`, `5B.10`

**Search gap**
- I found strong evidence for **institutionalization in finance, child policy, and administrative reform**, but less direct evidence of a new durable **national human-rights institution** or other deep equality institutions being completed in 2024.
- The clearest durable structures are **procedural** and **budgetary** rather than transformative social-welfare institutions.
- Some reforms were clearly underway, but several remained partial, contested, or dependent on future legislation and implementation.
